title: Supernova Remnant DEM L316
caption: The supernova remnant DEM L316, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Michaud, S. Fisher, R. Carrasco & T. Rector (Univ. of Alaska at Anchorage)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A peanut-shaped nebula dominates this image from the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South. It is DEM L316, a vast cloud complex in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Although it looks like a single object, recent research indicates that DEM L316 is really two separate clouds of gas and dust, each created by a different type of supernova explosion.

Supernovae come in more than one kind. Some happen when a massive star runs out of fuel and its core collapses; others occur when a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a smaller star, is pushed past its limit and blows apart. Each kind leaves behind an expanding shell of debris, and the shells can differ in the chemical elements they contain. From our viewpoint, the two clouds in DEM L316 blend together into what looks like one peanut-shaped nebula.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini South through [O III], S II and hydrogen-alpha filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of specific gases, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye.
